title: Praying for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43–46)
hookLine: Judas Maccabeus sends an offering for the fallen; Catholics see here the practice of praying for the dead

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO FOR THEM NOW?
cards: Judas Maccabeus has led a Jewish revolt against a Greek king who tried to stamp out their faith. After one battle, his men go out the next day to gather their fallen friends and bring them home for burial.
And under the coats of the slain they find small objects consecrated to the idols of a nearby city, things the law forbade. Amulets, maybe. Charms for luck in battle.
Suddenly everyone understands why these men fell. What do you do for the dead now?

teach.h: THEY PRAYED FOR THE SIN TO BE FORGOTTEN.
teach.b: They don't condemn them and walk away. They pray that the sin be forgotten.
Then Judas takes up a collection among the soldiers and sends silver to Jerusalem, for a sacrifice for the sins of the dead.
And the writer stops to explain: if he hadn't hoped that the fallen would rise again, it would have been pointless to pray for the dead.
Then the line that gives us our carry, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."
Wholesome is the Latin salubris: health-giving, good for you.
The Catholic Church points to this passage when it teaches that those who die in God's friendship but still need purifying can be helped by the prayers of the living, the teaching called purgatory.
That's why Catholics have Masses said for the dead, pray for the souls in purgatory, and keep All Souls' Day for remembering them all. The Orthodox also pray for the dead.
Protestant churches differ among themselves on it, and Protestant Bibles, if they print Maccabees at all, place it among the Apocrypha. Now a look back.
This week: the Benedicite, the books between, Raphael on the road, a wedding night prayer, Judith, the hand of God, and prayers for the dead.

teach.h: FIFTY DAYS OF KINGS AND PROPHETS.
teach.b: And fifty days of Deborah, Gideon, Ruth, Hannah, Samuel, David, Solomon, Elijah, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Jonah, Job, the wisdom books and the seven.

how: Catholics have Masses offered for the dead, pray for the souls in purgatory, and keep All Souls' Day, and 2 Maccabees 12:43–46 is among the readings for funerals and Masses for the dead.

games.q: you're Judas Maccabeus. your fallen men are found wearing charms the law forbade. what do you do?
o: condemn them and leave them where they lie.
pray for them, and send an offering to Jerusalem for their sins.
hide what you found and say nothing.
games.why: they pray that the sin be forgotten, and Judas sends silver for a sacrifice for the dead: a holy and wholesome thought.

practice: Let the people you've lost come to mind, one at a time, and say each name quietly as it comes: grandparents, parents, friends, someone who died young, someone you had unfinished business with.
Don't hold back the complicated ones; Judas didn't. If you pray, ask God's mercy on each name, as Catholics do; if you don't, let naming them be enough.

wordCard.voice: Judas Maccabeus. He sent an offering for his fallen soldiers after amulets were found on their bodies, and Catholics see here the practice of praying for the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: holy and wholesome (health-giving), the Vulgate's words in 2 Maccabees 12:46.

carryVoice: Your line: a holy and wholesome thought. Prayer that reaches past the grave, in hope. Day four hundred forty-one, and a block, done.
